blogDetails.title: Building Products That People Actually Use
blogDetails.excerpt: Good software is not just about writing clean code. It is about understanding people, solving the right problems, and making something worth returning to.

content.text: Most software fails not because the code is bad, but because the product was built for the wrong person or the wrong problem. I have made this mistake more times than I care to admit — shipping features that nobody asked for, designing screens that solved my problem and not the user's.
Start With a Real Problem

Before you write a single line of code, you need to answer one question honestly: does anyone actually have this problem? Not 'would they like this feature', not 'this would be cool', but: do real people run into this friction regularly enough that they would change their habits for a solution?

content.alt: A whiteboard with user journey mapping
content.caption: Good products begin on a whiteboard, not in a code editor.

content.text: A product that solves a real problem for ten people is infinitely more valuable than a product that almost solves an imaginary problem for ten thousand.
content.author: Paul Graham (paraphrased)

content.text: The Three Filters
I have started running every product decision through three filters before committing to it. They are simple questions, but they cut through a lot of noise.

items: Is this solving a real, recurring pain for a specific person?
Is there evidence (not assumption) that this matters to them?
Would removing this feature make the product significantly worse?

content.text: What Good Products Have in Common

content.caption: Common traits of products people return to
rows: You can explain it in one sentence
Does not waste the user's attention
More value the longer you use it
Obsidian: your notes become a brain

content.text: Shipping Is Not the End

The version you ship on launch day is the worst version of your product that will ever exist. The real work starts after. Listening to how people actually use it, watching where they get confused, noticing what they never touch — that is the feedback loop that turns good software into something people genuinely rely on.

items: Read every support message as a product signal
Watch session recordings without judgment
Talk to churned users — they tell you the truth
Ship small, ship often, pay attention

content.text: Building products that people actually use is not a skill you develop once and keep forever. It is a practice — a daily discipline of staying curious about people, honest about assumptions, and humble enough to change course when the evidence points somewhere unexpected.

blogDetails.title: A Practical Guide to Next.js Project Structure
blogDetails.excerpt: How I think about organizing components, features, data, and routes when building larger Next.js applications.

content.text: When a Next.js project grows past a certain point — somewhere around ten routes and fifteen components — the default structure starts to feel cramped. Files get lost. Imports become guessing games. Refactoring turns into archaeology.

After working on several production Next.js applications, I have settled on a structure that scales well without being overly prescriptive. It is not a framework — just a set of sensible defaults that can flex when the project demands it.
The Top-Level Structure

content.code:
src/
├── app/              # Next.js App Router (routes only)
│   ├── (main)/       # Grouped layout routes
│   │   ├── about/
│   │   ├── blogs/
│   │   └── work/
│   ├── api/          # API route handlers
│   ├── globals.css
│   └── layout.tsx
├── components/       # Shared, reusable UI components
├── screens/          # Page-level screen components
├── data/             # Static JSON data files
├── hooks/            # Custom React hooks
├── lib/              # Utility functions & helpers
├── services/         # API client functions
└── providers/        # Context & global providers

content.text: The app/ Directory — Routes Only

With the App Router, I treat the app/ directory as a routing layer only. Page files stay thin — they import a screen component, pass props, and render. No business logic, no fetch logic, no JSX beyond what is strictly necessary for the layout.
Screens vs Components
This is the distinction that saves the most confusion. A component is reusable anywhere. A screen is a full-page layout that belongs to one specific route.

content.caption: When to put something in components/ vs screens/
rows: Used in more than one page?

content.text: Data Files
For portfolio sites, personal projects, and small applications, static JSON in data/ is often the right call. No database overhead, no API layer, full type safety with TypeScript imports.

items: Keep one concern per file (projects.json, blogs.json, etc.)
Export arrays under a named key, not as a root array
Co-locate TypeScript types in a types/ or lib/ file
Validate shape at the import level with Zod if data is dynamic

content.text: The best project structure is the one your team can navigate without asking questions.
content.author: A principle worth remembering

content.text: None of this is absolute. The structure above reflects what works for my projects. Yours might need something different. The goal is not to follow a template — it is to make intentional decisions early, so you spend less time reorganizing and more time building.

blogDetails.title: My Favorite React Patterns
blogDetails.excerpt: A collection of React patterns that help me write components that are easier to understand, maintain, and evolve.

content.text: After years of building React applications, certain patterns keep showing up in the cleanest, most maintainable codebases. These are not tricks or hacks — they are structural approaches that make components easier to reason about, test, and extend.
1. Compound Components
Compound components let you express complex UI relationships through JSX composition, without prop-drilling or clunky configuration objects.

content.code:
<Accordion>
  <Accordion.Item value="one">
    <Accordion.Trigger>What is this?</Accordion.Trigger>
    <Accordion.Content>
      A compound component pattern.
    </Accordion.Content>
  </Accordion.Item>
</Accordion>

content.text: 2. Container / Presentational Split
Separate the logic from the rendering. A container component handles data fetching, state, and side effects. A presentational component renders UI from props and nothing else.
3. Custom Hooks for Logic Reuse
Any time I find myself duplicating logic across two components, it goes into a custom hook. Hooks are the cleanest unit of abstraction React has.
Patterns to Use With Care

items: Higher-Order Components (HOCs) — hooks usually do it better
Context for all state — Context re-renders are broad
Deeply nested compound components — keep trees shallow
Over-abstracting early — wait for the pattern to emerge naturally

content.text: Write the simplest thing that could possibly work. Reach for patterns only when the code tells you it needs them.
content.author: Abdullah Al Maksud

blogDetails.title: Designing for Developers
blogDetails.excerpt: You do not need to become a professional designer to build interfaces that feel thoughtful, clear, and intentional.

content.text: Most developers think design is about aesthetics — about making things look nice. It is not. Design is about communication. A well-designed interface communicates clearly.
The Rules That Matter Most

items: Use spacing generously — white space is not empty space
Limit your type scale to 4-5 sizes
Pick one accent color and use it with restraint
Align everything — random alignment looks amateur
Reduce, then reduce again — remove anything the user does not need

content.text: Type Scale Reference

content.caption: A minimal type scale for developer-built UIs
Good spacing and consistent alignment are 80% of the battle.

content.text: Tools That Help

items: Figma — design before you build, always
Coolors.co — fast, harmonious color palette generation
Fontpair.co — find font combinations that work
Refactoring UI (book) — the best design resource for developers

content.text: Good design is not magic. It is the result of applying a small number of principles consistently. Start there, and the aesthetics will follow.

blogDetails.title: Why I Still Love Making Things
blogDetails.excerpt: A personal reflection on programming, designing, writing, and the strange joy of turning an idea into something real.

content.text: There is a moment in every project — usually somewhere between the rough idea and the working prototype — where something clicks. The logic connects. The design starts to feel right.
The act of making something real from nothing — even something small — is one of the most quietly satisfying things a person can do.
content.author: Abdullah Al Maksud

content.text: What Making Feels Like

Programming is the closest thing to having a superpower. You type words and machines do things. The feedback loop is fast, the medium is infinitely flexible, and the barrier between imagination and reality is lower than it has ever been.

content.alt: A developer at work, surrounded by sketches and notes
content.caption: Making things is both deeply personal and endlessly collaborative.

content.text: The Things I Make

items: Software products — because good tools make lives easier
Design systems — because consistency is a form of respect
Written work — because ideas deserve to be expressed precisely
Side projects — because curiosity deserves to be followed

content.text: When Making Gets Hard

Not every day feels like momentum. Some days the code does not cooperate. The design feels wrong no matter how many times you adjust it. On those days, I remind myself that the hard part is not the skill — it is the showing up.
If you make things — code, design, writing, music, furniture, food — keep going. The world is better for the things people bother to make well.

blogDetails.title: The Tools I Use Every Day
blogDetails.excerpt: A look at the tools, frameworks, and small utilities that are part of my everyday workflow as a developer and designer.

content.text: Good tools do not make you a better developer. But bad tools will slow you down, frustrate you, and make the work feel harder than it needs to be.
Development Stack

content.caption: My core development stack
rows: Types catch errors before users do
Design tokens as utilities, fast iteration

content.text: Design Tools

items: Figma — everything design related, from wireframes to polished UI
Unsplash — high quality images when needed
Lucide Icons — clean, consistent icon set with React support
Google Fonts — Inter and Outfit for most projects

content.text: Productivity

items: Notion — notes, project docs, and long-form thinking
Linear — issue tracking for anything that needs to ship
Raycast — app launcher, clipboard manager, everything
Arc Browser — the best browser I have used in a decade

content.caption: The setup matters less than the consistency of showing up.

content.text: What I Have Dropped

I used to chase every new tool. I have stopped. The best tool is the one you actually use. Switching has a hidden cost — setup time, migration effort, and the mental overhead of learning something new.

items: Stopped: Obsidian (too much configuration for my needs)
Stopped: Jira (overkill for solo and small-team work)
Stopped: Webpack direct config (Next.js handles it better)
Stopped: CSS-in-JS (Tailwind is faster to iterate)

content.text: The goal is not to have the best tools. The goal is to remove the friction between having an idea and making it real.
content.author: Abdullah Al Maksud
